Platform Proposal Prepared for Bunce Performing Arts

One home for
everything Bunce.

Today your season lives in six places — the website, Discord, email, Google Forms, a giving app, and whichever spreadsheet someone remembered to update. This proposal replaces all of it with a single portal that cast, crew, families, volunteers, donors, and staff each log into once and find exactly what they need.

Timed to your 20th Anniversary Season. A four-week MVP starting this fall puts the platform live well before your Kickoff Cabaret — so the anniversary season is the first one Bunce runs entirely on its own system.

The situation today

You've outgrown the tools, not the other way around.

Bunce has done something genuinely impressive with the tools available — twenty years of shows, camps, and programs, run by volunteers, mostly on free software. Nothing here is broken. What's happened is simpler: six separate tools can't share what they each know, so the job of connecting them quietly falls to people.

Website

A warm front door for audiences. Shows the season, the team, and the camps.

Where it stopsIt was built to welcome an audience, not to hold a family's details. Since nobody signs in, personal things — call times, forms, photos — have to live somewhere else.
Discord

Fast, informal chatter between cast and crew during a run.

Where it stopsWonderful in the moment, harder to return to. Announcements scroll past, and families who aren't on Discord don't see them at all.
Email

Calls, rehearsal updates, and schedule changes go out to the cast list.

Where it stopsDependable for sending, but it can't tell you who has read it — so a last-minute change always needs a backup plan.
Google Forms

Auditions, camp registration, volunteer interest, and conflict forms.

Where it stopsCollects beautifully, then stops. Answers land in a sheet that doesn't know about anything else, so families are asked for the same details each season.
Giving app

Collects donations at shows and during the year.

Where it stopsDoes its job, just separately. A donor and a cast parent are often the same person, and neither system can know it.
Spreadsheets & paper

The quiet glue that holds the rest together.

Where it stopsIt works because a few generous people carry it in their heads. That's a lot to ask of volunteers, and it's hard to hand on.
For a parent

"Is call 5:30 or 6:00?" There are a few places that might say, and no way to tell which is current — so most people just ask someone directly.

For a volunteer

Someone glad to help with concessions may not know which nights are short. Without somewhere to see that, willing hands go unused.

For staff

One schedule change gets typed into Discord, email, and the website — and then answered again for anyone who missed all three.

The proposal

The Bunce Hub — one login, one source of truth.

One platform, on your own domain, wearing your own brand. Everyone gets the same front door and sees the version of it that belongs to them. Information gets entered once and shows up everywhere it's relevant — because it's all the same system.

Who logs in, and what they see

Cast & crew calls, scripts, conflicts, calendar
Families registration, forms, photos, payments
Volunteers open shifts they can claim themselves
Donors & sponsors giving history, receipts, impact
Production team scene notes by department, with read receipts
Everyone messaging, and a directory of who's who
Staff & board everything, plus who's still missing what
Enter once

A family's contact info, allergies, and photo consent are entered a single time and carry across every show, camp, and BEAT session.

Reach everyone

One announcement goes out as a push notification, an email, and a post in the portal at the same time. You can see who's seen it.

Nothing scrolls away

Every call, form, photo, note, and announcement stays searchable — this season and five seasons from now.

Owned by Bunce

Your data, your domain, your accounts. No per-seat pricing, and nothing held hostage by a vendor.

Open the live prototype
Built for a youth organization

Photos of other people's children deserve real controls.

A gallery is the feature families will love most and the one most likely to cause a problem if it's built carelessly. This is designed so the safe thing happens by default, without anyone having to remember a policy.

Private by default

Albums are visible to signed-in cast families only. Making an album public is a deliberate, logged action taken by staff — never the default, and never something a parent can do accidentally.

Consent is enforced by the system

The photo release you already collect becomes a setting on the child's record. If a family declines, that child is automatically excluded from public albums and can't be tagged by others. Nobody has to remember who opted out.

Tagging a minor is restricted

Only a child's own parent or staff can tag that child. Any parent can request removal of a photo of their child with one tap, and it disappears from view immediately while staff review it.

Messages to a minor include a guardian

Adults can't message a performer under 18 privately. The child's parent or guardian is added to the conversation automatically, every time, with no way to switch it off. Messaging between adults works normally.

Comments are attributable

Everyone posts under their real name and role — there are no anonymous accounts. Staff can moderate or lock comments on any album, and there is a full audit trail of uploads, tags, and removals.

How we'll work

Four weeks, four stages, nothing behind a curtain.

You'll see working software at the end of every week, not a status report. The stages below are sequential because each one's decisions feed the next — discovery determines what gets designed, and design determines what gets built.

Week 1 · Discovery

Learn how Bunce actually runs

  • Sit down with staff, a board member, a stage manager, and two cast parents
  • Walk through one full production start to finish — audition to strike
  • Inventory every form, list, spreadsheet, and vendor invoice you use today
  • Agree on what makes the MVP and what waits for phase two
You get A written scope with the MVP feature list, signed off before I build anything.
Week 2 · Design

Make it look and feel like Bunce

  • Clickable screens for every flow in the tour above
  • Your logo, colors, and voice applied throughout
  • Review session — you click through it and tell me what's wrong
  • Data model set up: families, performers, seasons, shows, shifts, gifts
You get A clickable prototype you can share with the board before a line of it is final.
Week 3 · Build

Stand up the real thing

  • Accounts, roles, and permissions
  • Portal, calendar, announcements, push notifications
  • Registration and audition sign-ups
  • Gallery with tagging, comments, and consent enforcement
  • Donations live through Stripe
You get A working site on a private link, updated daily as it comes together.
Week 4 · Launch

Move you in and hand over the keys

  • Import your current families, donors, and season calendar
  • Train staff and board — one live session, recorded
  • Written how-to guides for the four most common tasks
  • Go live on your domain, with a soft launch to staff first
You get A live platform, your data inside it, and a team that knows how to run it.
What I need from Bunce

About four hours total across the month: one discovery session, one design review, one training session, and a single named decision-maker who can answer questions within a day or two. That's genuinely it.

How we stay in sync

A short written update every Friday with what shipped, what's next, and anything I need from you. Plus a live link that's always current, so you're never waiting on a demo to see progress.

After the MVP

About a mobile app.

Short version: you almost certainly want the first option, not the second, and the first one is cheap. Both are listed honestly so the board can decide rather than guess.

Recommended · $500

Installable app (PWA)

A family taps "Add to Home Screen" once. After that the Hub has its own icon, opens full-screen with no browser bar, and can send push notifications — on both iPhone and Android. It is the same platform you're already paying for, finished properly.

Why this first: it costs about ten hours, there is no app store review, and an update reaches everyone the moment I publish it. No one has to remember to update anything.

Optional · $4,500–6,000

Native iOS & Android app

A real app in the App Store and Google Play, built on the same platform and data. Three to four weeks. Add roughly $124 in the first year for developer accounts ($99/yr Apple, $25 once for Google), then a few hours a year keeping up with OS releases.

The one real argument for it: on iPhone, push notifications only work after a family adds the Hub to their home screen. A native app removes that step. If a meaningful number of your families never do it, that's when this becomes worth the money — and you'll know within a season.

Later additionsWhat it gives youInvestment
Installable app (PWA) Home-screen icon, full screen, push notificationsRecommended before anything native $500
Native iOS & Android app Store presence, push with no setup step for familiesPlus ~$124/yr in store fees $4,500–6,000

Or simply as needed Anything smaller, billed only for hours worked $50 / hour

None of this is required for the platform to be useful — the MVP works on a phone browser on day one. These are priced now so nothing later comes as a surprise, and every one of them is optional forever.

Why me

I build zero-to-one products for a living.

I'm a product manager who takes products from nothing to launched — connecting what people actually need, what the organization requires, and what can realistically be built, then making sure it ships. I've done this for medical records platforms, provider networks, and commission systems where the details genuinely mattered.

A volunteer-run theater company is a harder design problem than most enterprise software, because nobody has time to be trained and everyone is a volunteer at 7 PM on a Tuesday. That constraint is the whole design brief: if a cast parent can't figure it out on their phone in the parking lot, it has failed.

I've also built and launched a long run of websites for small organizations and independent businesses, so the practical side — domains, hosting, email, payments, getting a thing actually live — is well-worn ground rather than a research project.

I'm local, I'm reachable, and I'd rather build one thing that Bunce actually uses every day than a long list of features nobody opens.
